name: Mahalakshminathar Temple, Tirunindriyur
deity: Shiva as Mahalakshminathar (Mahalakshmeeswarar), with the goddess Loka Nayaki (Ulaga Nayaki)
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine of the Chola country, sung in the Tevaram (7th century); said to have been a Maadakoil in the Tevaram age, with later renovation
dynasty: Early Chola tradition (Kochchengat Chola), with later patrons
summary: Mahalakshminathar is the Shiva of Tirunindriyur, the Tevaram shrine between Mayiladuthurai and Sirkazhi where Mahalakshmi, consort of Vishnu, is remembered to have worshipped the Lord, and where a lamp that would not burn in the forest led a king to a buried linga.

sections.history: Tirunindriyur lies on the road from Mayiladuthurai towards Sirkazhi, in the Chola country north of the Kaveri, and its Shiva temple is a Paadal Petra Sthalam praised by all three great Tevaram poets: Sambandar and Appar each sang a decad here, and Sundarar two, one of which survives only in part. Tradition holds that in the age of the hymns the shrine stood as a Maadakoil, the raised temple form associated with the early Chola king Kochchengat Chola. About a century ago the Nagarathar community undertook a major renovation, giving the complex its present layout. The name of the town is read in two ways: as the place where Tiru, Lakshmi, stayed, and as the place where the wick, thiri, stood still.
sections.architecture: A three-tiered rajagopuram marks the entrance to the temple. Within, the sanctum houses the linga of Mahalakshminathar, who is also called Lakshmipureeswarar, Jamadhagneesar and Parikeshwarar, and the goddess Loka Nayaki, also called Ulaga Nayaki, is honoured in her own shrine. The sacred tank is known as Neela Poigai. Though the early Maadakoil character is a matter of tradition, the present complex bears the stamp of the Nagarathar renovation of the last century, a clear and orderly plan of the Dravidian type. Finer measurements of the towers and sanctum were not verified.
sections.legends: The temple keeps several stories. In the best known, Mahalakshmi, consort of Vishnu, worshipped Shiva here, and so the Lord is called Mahalakshmeeswarar; the goddess of fortune is thus remembered as a devotee at the feet of the Lord whom Vishnu himself reveres. Another tells of a Chola king who travelled each day to worship at Chidambaram. Every night, as his party crossed a forest on this road, the torches went out, and relit once the forest was behind them. The king learned that a holy linga lay buried there, uncovered it, and raised a temple. The wick that stood still, thiri nindra, is one of the explanations given for the name. The sage Jamadagni, Parashurama, who was freed of the sin of killing his mother, Indra, Agastya and the elephant Airavata are also remembered as worshippers here.
sections.festivals: The principal festivals are Aani Tirumanjanam in the month of Aani (June or July), Maha Shivaratri in February or March, and Tirukarthikai in November or December. Pradosham and other monthly observances are kept as at every Shiva temple. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Tamil calendar.
sections.experience: Tirunindriyur suits a quiet half-day on the Mayiladuthurai road, and combines easily with a visit to nearby Vaitheeswarankoil. Pass beneath the three-tiered gateway, offer prayer to Mahalakshminathar, and then to the goddess Loka Nayaki in her shrine. Many devotees come with a prayer for prosperity and household well-being, in the memory of Mahalakshmi's worship, and linger by the tank, Neela Poigai. The village around the temple is small, and the atmosphere is still and unhurried, in keeping with a shrine sung by all three Tevaram saints.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; published timings differ, so confirm locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tirunindriyur is about 7 km from Mayiladuthurai on the road towards Sirkazhi, and about 6 km from Vaitheeswarankoil; some listings give a slightly longer distance from Mayiladuthurai, which is also the nearest major railway station. Buses and taxis on the Mayiladuthurai–Sirkazhi road serve the village. Tiruchirappalli is the nearest large airport, well over 100 km away.
